title: AI in Excel 1: built-in AI and Copilot

lessons.title: The AI tools in Excel and when to use each
learn: Flash Fill, Analyze Data, Copilot, Agent Mode, Claude
What each is good and bad at

lessons.title: Analyze Data
lessons.mac:
Excel for Mac: Home tab > Analyze Data (far right).
Not visible? Sign in with your Microsoft 365 account and update Excel (Help > Check for Updates).

steps.say: This is where we are headed. A sales register with sixty orders, and next to it a revenue-by-region chart that Excel suggested on its own. When your manager asks a quick question about a sheet, Analyze Data gives you a first answer in seconds, with no formulas.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S18-02 Done

steps.say: In this lesson you'll ask Analyze Data questions in plain English, insert a suggested PivotTable or chart, and check one answer with a formula. Practice sheet: S18-02.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Open Analyze Data from the Home tab
• Ask questions in plain English
• Insert a suggested PivotTable or chart
• Check the answer with SUMIFS
Practice sheet: S18-02

steps.say: Analyze Data is the older, built-in AI in Excel. It comes with Microsoft 365 and needs no Copilot licence. It works best on a clean table with one header row, and it only answers questions about numbers in that table.

acts.t:
Analyze Data (Home tab)
• Free with Microsoft 365, no Copilot licence
• Needs a tidy table: one header row, no blank rows
• Suggests charts, PivotTables and patterns
• Answers questions like: total Revenue by Region

steps.say: Go to the practice sheet S18-02. The data runs from A1 to H61: date, region, state, city, category, salesperson, units and revenue. Click any cell inside the table.
On the Home tab, click Analyze Data. A pane opens on the right with a question box at the top and a few suggestions Excel has already found.
Scroll through the suggestions. Each card is a chart or a small PivotTable built from your data. Excel picks these by looking for big differences and trends, so they change with your data.
Now ask your own question. In the box at the top, type: total revenue by region. Press Return.

acts.h: Set Ask a question about your data to total revenue by region

steps.say: Excel answers with a chart or a table. Look at the bar for West. Remember that figure, because we will check it in a moment.
Under the answer, click Insert PivotTable. Excel adds a new sheet with a ready PivotTable. If you only see Insert Chart, that's fine too. Both are real objects you can edit later.
Let's ask a sharper question. Type: revenue by category for Maharashtra, and press Return. You can mix column names and values from the data in one sentence.

acts.h: Set Ask a question about your data to revenue by category for Maharashtra

steps.say: Now check the AI's work. Close the pane. In cell K1, type equals SUMIFS, open bracket, H2 colon H61 for revenue, comma, B2 colon B61 for region, comma, quote West quote, close bracket.
Press Return. K1 shows ₹28,49,320. Compare it with the West bar in the Analyze Data answer. When the two match, you can trust the chart. When they don't, look for a filter or a blank row.

A common mistake is running Analyze Data on a sheet with merged headers or a blank row in the middle. Excel then sees two tables, or no table, and says it can't find patterns. Fix the layout first, then try again.

acts.t:
Common mistake
Analyze Data says “no patterns found” or gives odd answers.
• Remove blank rows and merged header cells
• Keep one header row with clear names
• Convert the range to a Table with Command T

steps.say: A pro tip: name your columns the way you speak. A header called Revenue gets better answers than one called Col H or Amt1.

acts.t:
Pro tip
Rename headers in plain words: Revenue, Region, Order date.
Analyze Data and Copilot both read your headers to understand the question.

steps.say: On Excel for Mac, Analyze Data sits in the same place: Home tab, far right. If you don't see it, check that you're signed in with your Microsoft 365 account.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Excel for Mac: Home tab > Analyze Data (far right).
Not visible? Sign in with your Microsoft 365 account and update Excel (Help > Check for Updates).

steps.say: To recap. Analyze Data answers plain-English questions on a clean table. You can insert its PivotTables and charts with one click. And you always check one number with your own formula.

acts.t:
Recap
• Home > Analyze Data, then ask in plain English
• Insert the suggested PivotTable or chart
• Check one figure with SUMIFS before you share it

steps.say: Your challenge: ask Analyze Data which salesperson has the highest revenue, insert the answer, and confirm it with a SUMIFS on the salesperson column. The Done sheet shows the region version.

acts.t:
Challenge
On sheet S18-02, ask: which salesperson has the highest revenue?
Insert the result, then check it with SUMIFS on column F.
Compare with sheet S18-02 Done.

lessons.title: Copilot setup on Mac
lessons.mac:
Excel for Mac: Excel menu > About Excel shows your version.
File > Account (or Excel > Preferences > Account) shows which licence is active.
Command Q fully quits; closing the window is not enough.

steps.say: Here's the finished setup: a plain list of expense claims turned into an Excel Table, saved on OneDrive, with Copilot ready on the Home tab. Most Copilot problems at work come from missing one of these steps.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S18-03 Done

steps.say: You'll learn the four things Copilot needs, how to turn a range into a Table, and how to fix a greyed-out Copilot button. Practice sheet: S18-03.

acts.t:
You will learn
• What Copilot needs: licence, OneDrive, AutoSave, clean data
• Turn a range into a Table with Command T
• Fix a greyed-out Copilot button
Practice sheet: S18-03

steps.say: Copilot needs four things. A licence: Microsoft 365 Copilot at work, or Personal, Family or Premium at home. The file on OneDrive or SharePoint. AutoSave switched on. And data in a tidy block, ideally a Table.

acts.t:
Copilot checklist
1. Licence: Microsoft 365 Copilot, or Personal / Family / Premium
2. Signed in with that same account
3. File on OneDrive or SharePoint, AutoSave on
4. Data in a clean block, ideally an Excel Table

steps.say: Look at the title bar. In Excel for the web the file always lives in OneDrive, so AutoSave is already on. On Excel for Mac, check that the AutoSave switch at the top left is on. If it's off, the file is probably saved on your Mac only.
The checklist is also typed on the sheet in column G, so you can keep it for later.
Now the data. A1 to E19 is a plain range of expense claims. Click A1, then press Command T to make it a Table.
The Create Table box shows the range. Make sure My table has headers is ticked, then click OK.
The range is now a Table with filter buttons and banded rows. Copilot reads Tables more reliably, because it knows exactly where the data starts and ends.
Now open Copilot from the Home tab and ask a simple question: what is the total Amount by Department? This first question tells you Copilot can see your data.

acts.t: What is the total Amount by Department in this table? Answer only, do not change anything.

steps.say: Copilot replies in the pane with a short summary and usually a small table. The exact wording will differ each time you ask. What matters is that it read the right table.
Quick check. Click G9 and type equals SUM, open bracket, E2 colon E19, close bracket, then press Return. Don't type directly under the Table, or Excel adds your total as a new row.
G9 shows ₹83,360. Add up Copilot's department figures. They should come to the same amount. If one department is missing, Copilot may have skipped a row with a typo in the department name.
Now the common problem: the Copilot button is greyed out. Here are the usual causes, in the order to check them.

acts.t:
Copilot greyed out? Check in this order
1. Wrong account: File > Account, sign in with the licensed one
2. File not on OneDrive, or AutoSave off
3. Licence just added: quit Excel fully (Command Q) and reopen
4. Old version: Help > Check for Updates
5. Data not readable: convert it to a Table

steps.say: One more cause on a work laptop: your IT team may not have assigned the Copilot licence yet. If the checklist looks fine and Copilot is still grey, send them a screenshot of File, Account.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Excel for Mac: Excel menu > About Excel shows your version.
File > Account (or Excel > Preferences > Account) shows which licence is active.
Command Q fully quits; closing the window is not enough.

steps.say: To recap. Copilot needs a licence, a file on OneDrive with AutoSave, and clean data. Command T turns a range into a Table. And if the button is grey, check the account, the save location and updates.

acts.t:
Recap
• Licence + OneDrive + AutoSave + clean data
• Command T makes a Table Copilot can read
• Greyed out: account, location, restart, update

steps.say: Your challenge: on the S18-03 sheet, ask Copilot for the total Amount by Expense head, then check the largest one with a SUMIFS. The Done sheet has the finished Table.

acts.t:
Challenge
Ask Copilot: total Amount by Expense head.
Check the biggest head with SUMIFS on column D.
Compare with sheet S18-03 Done.

steps.say: This is the finished sheet: twelve months of sales for four branches, a growth table, and a one-line insight that Pune grew fastest while Chennai had a spike in returns. Copilot found these, and we checked them.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S18-04 Done

steps.say: You'll learn to ask Copilot for summaries, trends and outliers, use follow-up questions, and verify the answer. Practice sheet: S18-04.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Ask for a summary, a trend and an outlier
• Use follow-up questions instead of starting over
• Check the answer with your own formula
Practice sheet: S18-04

steps.say: Chat mode only reads and answers. It does not change your sheet. A good question names the goal, the columns to use and the format you want back.

acts.t:
A good chat prompt
Goal: which branch grew fastest
Data: Revenue by Branch and Month
Output: a short table, then one sentence
Rule: chat mode reads, it does not edit

steps.say: Open sheet S18-04. The table runs from A1 to E49: month, branch, revenue, orders and returns for April 2025 to March 2026.
Open Copilot in Chat mode and ask: summarise total Revenue by Branch for the year and tell me which branch grew the fastest from April to March.

acts.t: Summarise total Revenue by Branch for the whole year, then tell me which Branch grew the fastest from April 2025 to March 2026. Show a short table.

steps.say: Copilot replies with a small table of branch totals and names the fastest-growing branch. Read the table carefully. Note the Pune total, because we will check it.
Now a follow-up, in the same chat. Ask: are there any months where Returns look unusually high compared with Orders? You don't need to repeat the table name, Copilot remembers the context.

acts.t: Are there any months where Returns look unusually high compared with Orders? Name the branch and month.

steps.say: Copilot points to the outlier it found and gives a reason. An outlier is only a lead. Your job is to look at the actual row before you report it.
Let's look. Filter or scroll to Chennai, November 2025. Click cell E34 to see the returns for that month.
Now check the Pune total. In H1 type equals SUMIFS, open bracket, C2 colon C49, comma, B2 colon B49, comma, quote Pune quote, close bracket, and press Return.
H1 shows ₹3,64,63,000. If Copilot's Pune figure is the same, good. If it's different, ask it which rows it used. Usually it has missed a filter or a month.

Same check for the outlier. In H2 type equals SUMIFS, open bracket, E2 colon E49, comma, B2 colon B49, comma, quote Chennai quote, comma, A2 colon A49, comma, DATE open bracket 2025 comma 11 comma 1, close bracket twice.
H2 shows 145 returns, several times a normal month. Now the insight is backed by a number you calculated yourself.
A common mistake is asking a vague question like: tell me about this data. You get a generic answer. Add the column names and what you want to decide, and the answer gets specific.

acts.t:
Common mistake
Vague: “Tell me about this data.”
Better: “Which Branch had the highest Revenue growth from Apr-25 to Mar-26? Show a table of Branch, Apr Revenue, Mar Revenue, growth %.”

steps.say: A pro tip: when an answer is useful, ask Copilot to add it to a new sheet. Then the summary stays in the file instead of only in the chat.

acts.t: Add the branch summary table you just made to a new sheet.

steps.say: To recap. Chat mode answers questions without editing. Follow-ups keep the context. And every number you plan to share gets a quick SUMIFS check.

acts.t:
Recap
• Chat mode: read and answer only
• Follow-up questions build on the last answer
• Check one total and one outlier yourself

steps.say: Your challenge: ask Copilot which branch has the highest average order value, Revenue divided by Orders, then check it with two SUMIFS. Compare with the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
Ask: which Branch has the highest average order value (Revenue ÷ Orders)?
Check with SUMIFS of Revenue ÷ SUMIFS of Orders.
Compare with sheet S18-04 Done.

steps.say: Here's the result. An order list where Copilot added an Amount column and a GST column that looks up the right rate for each category. Below the rate table, an old formula that Copilot explained in plain words.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S18-05 Done

steps.say: You'll learn to create formula columns from a sentence, explain a formula you inherited, and read every formula Copilot writes. Practice sheet: S18-05.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Describe a column, let Copilot write the formula
• Ask Copilot to explain an inherited formula
• Read and check every formula it adds
Practice sheet: S18-05

steps.say: Copilot writes ordinary Excel formulas. Once a formula is in the cell, it's yours. It recalculates without Copilot, and anyone can read it. That's why you always read it.

acts.t:
How Copilot formula columns work
• You describe the column in a sentence
• Copilot shows the formula and a preview
• You click Insert column
• The result is a normal formula you can read and edit

steps.say: Open sheet S18-05. Orders are in A1 to G21: order ID, date, customer, state, category, quantity and unit price. The GST rates are in L1 to M6.
Open Copilot in Edit mode and type: add a column called Amount that multiplies Qty by Unit price for every row.

acts.t: Add a column called Amount that multiplies Qty by Unit price for every row.

steps.say: Copilot adds the new column to the right of the table. If it shows a preview first, check the formula in the preview and accept it.
Click the first cell of the new column and look at the formula bar. You should see quantity times unit price for the same row. If the formula points somewhere else, press Command Z and ask again.
Now a lookup. Ask: add a column called GST that looks up the GST rate for the Category from the table in L1 to M6 and multiplies it by Amount.

acts.t: Add a column called GST that looks up the GST rate for each row's Category from the table in L1:M6 and multiplies it by Amount.

steps.say: Click the first GST cell and read the formula. Copilot usually writes XLOOKUP or INDEX and MATCH. Check three things: it looks up the category, it uses the rate column, and it multiplies by the amount.
Now check one amount by hand. In M13, type equals F2 star G2, and press Return.
M13 shows ₹10,892. It should match the first Amount Copilot calculated. One matching row doesn't prove every row, but a mismatch here tells you to stop.
Next, a formula you inherited. Cell L10 has a long SUMPRODUCT from last year's file. Ask Copilot in Chat mode: explain the formula in cell L10 step by step in simple words.

acts.t: Explain the formula in cell L10 step by step in simple words. What does it add up?

steps.say: Copilot breaks the formula into parts: it checks for Electronics, checks for Maharashtra, multiplies quantity by price, and adds up only the rows where both are true. Compare that with the formula bar yourself.

A common mistake is accepting a formula column without looking. Copilot can pick the wrong column when two headers sound alike, such as Amount and Unit price. Always click one result cell and read it.

acts.t:
Common mistake
Accepting a formula column without reading it.
• Click the first result cell
• Read the formula bar: right columns? right row?
• Check one row by hand
• Command Z undoes the change

steps.say: A pro tip: ask for the formula in your style. For example: use XLOOKUP, not VLOOKUP, and round to two decimals. Copilot follows these rules well.

acts.t:
Pro tip
Add rules to the prompt:
“Use XLOOKUP, not VLOOKUP. Round GST to 2 decimals. Return 0 if the category is missing.”

steps.say: To recap. Describe a column and Copilot writes the formula. Ask it to explain formulas you inherit. And read every formula, then check one row by hand.

acts.t:
Recap
• Edit mode: “Add a column called … that …”
• Chat mode: “Explain the formula in L10”
• Read the formula bar and check one row

steps.say: Your challenge: ask Copilot to add a column Total with GST that adds Amount and GST, then check the first row by hand. Compare with the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
Ask Copilot: add a column Total with GST = Amount + GST.
Check row 2 by hand.
Compare with sheet S18-05 Done.

lessons.title: Copilot to highlight, sort and filter

steps.say: This is the finished sheet: sales reps sorted by achievement, with everyone below target shaded light red. A sales head can read it in five seconds.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S18-06 Done

steps.say: You'll learn to apply conditional formatting by prompt, sort and filter by prompt, and find top and bottom performers. Practice sheet: S18-06.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Highlight rows with a sentence
• Sort and filter by prompt
• Ask for top and bottom performers
• Count the highlights yourself
Practice sheet: S18-06

steps.say: Copilot uses Excel's own conditional formatting, sort and filter. So whatever it does, you can see it and change it from the Home tab later.

acts.t:
What Copilot uses
• Conditional Formatting rules (Home > Conditional Formatting > Manage Rules)
• Sort and Filter on the table header buttons
Everything it adds stays editable

steps.say: Open sheet S18-06. Eighteen reps in A1 to E19: name, region, target, achieved and achievement percentage.
In Copilot, Edit mode, type: highlight the rows where Achieved is less than Target in light red.

acts.t: Highlight the entire rows where Achieved is less than Target in light red.

steps.say: Look at the sheet. Some rows are now shaded. Before trusting it, count them yourself.
In H1, type equals COUNTIF, open bracket, E2 colon E19, comma, quote less than 1 quote, close bracket. Achievement below one hundred percent means below target.
H1 shows 7. Count the red rows. If the numbers match, the rule is right. If not, open Home, Conditional Formatting, Manage Rules and read the rule Copilot created.
Now sort. Type: sort the table by Achievement percent from highest to lowest.

acts.t: Sort the table by Achievement % from highest to lowest.

steps.say: The best performer is now in row 2 and the weakest at the bottom. The red highlights moved with their rows, because the rule follows the data.
Now ask in Chat mode: who are the top three and bottom three reps by Achievement percent, and by how much did the bottom three miss target?

acts.t: Who are the top 3 and bottom 3 reps by Achievement %? For the bottom 3, how much did each miss Target by, in rupees?

steps.say: Compare the answer with the sorted table. Row 2 should be the top name and row 19 the bottom one. Today that is Aditya Joshi at the top and Rahul Verma at the bottom.
Now a filter. Type: show only the West region.

acts.t: Filter the table to show only the West region.

steps.say: Only the West reps are visible, and the region header shows a filter icon. A common mistake is forgetting the filter is on and then copying the data. The hidden rows don't come along.
Clear it. Ask Copilot to clear all filters, or click the filter button on Region and choose Clear Filter.

acts.t: Clear all filters on this table.

steps.say: To recap. Copilot highlights, sorts and filters with Excel's normal tools. Count the highlights with COUNTIF. And always clear filters before you share or copy data.

acts.t:
Recap
• “Highlight rows where …” creates a conditional formatting rule
• Sort and filter by prompt, undo with Command Z
• COUNTIF checks the highlights; clear filters before sharing

steps.say: Your challenge: ask Copilot to highlight achievement above one hundred and twenty percent in green, then check the count with COUNTIF. Compare with the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
Ask Copilot: highlight Achievement % above 120% in light green.
Check with =COUNTIF(E2:E19,">1.2").
Compare with sheet S18-06 Done.

steps.say: This is the result: revenue by region and category, and a column chart of revenue by region, all from eighty sales rows. Copilot builds the first version, and you refine it with follow-ups.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S18-07 Done

steps.say: You'll learn to create a PivotTable and a chart from a prompt, refine them with follow-ups, and check one figure. Practice sheet: S18-07.

acts.t:
You will learn
• PivotTable by prompt, on a new sheet
• Chart by prompt, then refine it
• Check one figure with SUMIFS
Practice sheet: S18-07

steps.say: A good chart prompt says what to show, how to group it, and what kind of chart. You can change any of it later with a follow-up, so start simple.

acts.t:
Chart and pivot prompts
What: total Revenue
By: Region (rows), Category (columns)
How: PivotTable on a new sheet / clustered column chart
Then refine: sort, title, colours

steps.say: Open sheet S18-07. Sales rows are in A1 to E81: date, region, category, channel and revenue.
In Copilot, Edit mode, type: create a PivotTable on a new sheet showing total Revenue with Region in rows and Category in columns.

acts.t: Create a PivotTable on a new sheet showing total Revenue with Region in rows and Category in columns.

steps.say: Copilot adds a new sheet with the PivotTable. Look at the row and column labels. There should be four regions down the side and three categories across the top, with a grand total.
Now a follow-up. Ask: add a clustered column chart of total Revenue by Region next to the PivotTable.

acts.t: Add a clustered column chart of total Revenue by Region next to the PivotTable.

steps.say: The chart appears. Now refine it rather than starting over. Ask: sort the regions from highest to lowest revenue and set the chart title to Revenue by region, FY 2025-26.

acts.t: Sort the regions from highest to lowest revenue and set the chart title to: Revenue by region, FY 2025-26.

steps.say: Check what changed. The tallest bar should be first, and the title should read exactly as you asked. If Copilot changed something else as well, press Command Z.
Now check one number. Go back to sheet S18-07. In H1 type equals SUMIFS, open bracket, E2 colon E81, comma, B2 colon B81, comma, quote South quote, close bracket, and press Return.
H1 shows ₹19,71,100. Compare it with the South grand total in the PivotTable. They should match exactly.
A common mistake: adding new rows to the data and expecting the PivotTable to change. A PivotTable doesn't update by itself. Click inside it and use PivotTable, Refresh, or ask Copilot to refresh it.

acts.t:
Common mistake
New data rows, old PivotTable numbers.
Fix: click the PivotTable > PivotTable tab > Refresh
(Excel for Mac: PivotTable Analyze > Refresh, or Command Option F5)

steps.say: A pro tip: if you need a chart that updates without refreshing, ask Copilot to build the summary with SUMIFS formulas instead of a PivotTable, like on the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Pro tip
Prompt: “Build the Region by Category summary with SUMIFS formulas, not a PivotTable, and chart it.”
Formulas update instantly; PivotTables need Refresh.

steps.say: To recap. Ask for a PivotTable or chart in one sentence. Refine it with follow-ups instead of starting over. And match one total against your own SUMIFS.

acts.t:
Recap
• One sentence: what, grouped by, which chart
• Follow-ups: sort, title, colours
• Check one total; refresh PivotTables after new data

steps.say: Your challenge: ask Copilot for a PivotTable of revenue by Channel and month, and a line chart of it. Check the Online total with SUMIFS. Compare with the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
Ask Copilot: PivotTable of Revenue by Channel and month, plus a line chart.
Check the Online total with SUMIFS on column D.
Compare with sheet S18-07 Done.

lessons.title: Copilot for cleaning and text
learn: Classify feedback, extract details, fix inconsistencies

steps.say: Here's the result. Twenty customer feedback tickets with messy dates, names and state codes, now cleaned, with a sentiment, an issue type and the order number pulled out of the text. Work that used to take an afternoon.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S18-08 Done

steps.say: You'll learn to classify feedback, extract details from text, standardise state names and fix dates, all from the Copilot pane. Practice sheet: S18-08.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Classify feedback: sentiment and issue
• Extract an order number from text
• Standardise state names and dates
• Spot-check what Copilot changed
Practice sheet: S18-08

steps.say: A quick history note. Until September 2026 there was a COPILOT worksheet function that did this inside a cell. Microsoft retired it on fourteenth September 2026, and it never left preview. The same jobs now happen in the Copilot pane.

acts.t:
The =COPILOT() function: retired
• Prompt-in-a-cell function, preview only
• Retired 14 September 2026 (Microsoft MC1454373)
• Its jobs moved to the Copilot pane and to Claude in Excel:
  classify, extract, standardise, summarise text

steps.say: Open sheet S18-08. Look at the mess: dates in six formats, names in capitals and small letters, and states written as MH, maharashtra, Maharastra and so on.
Start with sentiment. In Copilot, Edit mode, type: add a column Sentiment that classifies each Feedback as Positive, Negative or Neutral.

acts.t: Add a column called Sentiment that classifies each Feedback as Positive, Negative or Neutral.

steps.say: Copilot adds the column. Read a few rows against the feedback text. Mixed comments, like the one about the colour being slightly different, are where AI and people disagree most.
Next, the issue. Give Copilot a fixed list so the answers stay consistent: Delivery, Product quality, Billing, Customer service, App or website, or Other.

acts.t: Add a column called Issue that picks the main topic of each Feedback from this list only: Delivery, Product quality, Billing, Customer service, App or website, Other.

steps.say: Now extraction. Ask: add a column Order No that extracts the order number starting with OD from the Feedback, or leaves it blank if there is none.

acts.t: Add a column called Order No that extracts the order number starting with OD from the Feedback text, or leaves it blank if there is none.

steps.say: Now the state names. Ask: standardise the State column to full official state names, for example MH becomes Maharashtra.

acts.t: Standardise the State column to full official Indian state or union territory names, for example MH becomes Maharashtra and Orissa becomes Odisha.

steps.say: Check the state column. Every row should now have a full name, and the old name Orissa should read Odisha. Gurgaon's state code HR should become Haryana, not Himachal Pradesh.
Last, the dates. Ask: convert the Date column to real dates shown as DD-MM-YYYY. The dates were written the Indian way, day first.

acts.t: Convert the Date column to real Excel dates shown as DD-MM-YYYY. The text dates were written day first, the Indian way.

steps.say: This is the common mistake to catch. The first ticket was written 03 slash 04 slash 2025, which means third April. Click B2. If it shows fourth March, Copilot read it the American way. Press Command Z and repeat that the dates are day first.

Now read three rows end to end: the sentiment, the issue and the order number. Ticket 1003 should be Negative, Billing, OD45907. If two of three rows look right, still check the rest before you report counts.
A pro tip: for long feedback lists, ask Copilot to write a short summary on a new sheet: the count by issue and three example quotes. It is faster to review than three hundred rows.

acts.t: On a new sheet, summarise the feedback: count of tickets by Issue and Sentiment, and two example comments for the most common negative issue.

steps.say: To recap. The Copilot pane now does the text jobs the COPILOT function used to do. Give fixed lists for categories. And always check day-first dates and a few rows by eye.

acts.t:
Recap
• Classify, extract and standardise from the Copilot pane
• Fixed category lists give consistent answers
• Check Indian dates (day first) and read a few rows

steps.say: Your challenge: ask Copilot to proper-case the Customer names and remove double spaces, then check rows 2 and 8. Compare with the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
Ask Copilot: put Customer names in proper case and remove extra spaces.
Check “ramesh iyer” and “deepak  singh”.
Compare with sheet S18-08 Done.

lessons.title: Copilot with Python: advanced analysis
lessons.mac:
Python in Excel on Mac: Microsoft 365, current channel.
Insert a Python cell: Formulas > Insert Python, or Control + Option + Shift + P.
Code runs in the Microsoft cloud, not on your Mac.

steps.say: This is the result: three years of monthly revenue with a trend chart, and a customer list ready for segmenting. Copilot writes Python in Excel to forecast and cluster, and you read what it did.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S18-09 Done

steps.say: You'll learn to ask for a forecast and a customer segmentation, then read the Python Copilot wrote. Practice sheet: S18-09.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Forecast revenue by prompt (Python in Excel)
• Group customers into segments
• Read the Python code it wrote
• Sanity-check the forecast
Practice sheet: S18-09

steps.say: Advanced analysis is a Copilot skill that writes Python and runs it in Microsoft's cloud. The results land on a new sheet as Python cells. You need Python in Excel on your plan.

acts.t:
Advanced analysis with Python
• Copilot writes =PY() cells on a new sheet
• Code runs in the Microsoft cloud (pandas, statsmodels, scikit-learn)
• Needs Python in Excel on your Microsoft 365 plan
• Results are a starting point, not a final answer

steps.say: Open sheet S18-09. Monthly revenue and marketing spend are in A1 to C37, April 2023 to March 2026. Customers are in E1 to H31 with annual spend, orders and days since the last order.
In Copilot, ask: using Python, forecast monthly Revenue for the next six months from the Monthly table, and show the forecast with a chart.

acts.t: Using Python, forecast monthly Revenue for the next 6 months from the Monthly1809 table, keep the Oct-Nov festive peak in mind, and show actuals and forecast on one chart.

steps.say: Copilot may ask to start advanced analysis. Allow it. It then adds a new sheet with Python cells, a forecast table and a chart. This takes a little longer than a normal answer.
Look at the forecast numbers on the new sheet. Before you believe them, compare them with recent history. Go back to sheet S18-09.
In J2, type equals AVERAGE, open bracket, B26 colon B37, close bracket. That's the average of the last twelve months.
J2 shows ₹56,17,750. A sensible forecast should sit near this level, a little higher if the trend is rising. If Copilot forecasts double or half of this, question the model.
Now segmentation. Ask: using Python, group the customers into three segments using Annual spend, Orders and Days since last order, and describe each segment.

acts.t: Using Python, group the customers in the Cust1809 table into 3 segments using Annual spend, Orders and Days since last order. Describe each segment in one line and list its customers.

steps.say: Copilot usually uses k-means clustering. You'll see three groups, typically loyal high spenders, occasional buyers and customers who are drifting away. The names it gives are its own guess.
Now read the Python. Ask Copilot: show the Python code you used and explain each step in plain English.

acts.t: Show the Python code you used for the segmentation and explain each step in plain English.

steps.say: Look for three things in the code: which columns it read with the x l function, whether it scaled the numbers before clustering, and how many clusters it chose. If any of these is wrong, say so in a follow-up.

acts.t:
Reading Copilot's Python
• xl("Cust1809[#All]") = which data it read
• StandardScaler = numbers put on the same scale
• KMeans(n_clusters=3) = how many groups
• Forecast: which model (e.g. ExponentialSmoothing) and seasonal period 12

steps.say: A common mistake is treating the forecast as fact. Three years of data is a short history, and a festive season can move a lot. Use the forecast as a range, not a promise.

acts.t:
Common mistake
Treating a forecast as a target.
• Ask Copilot for a low and high range
• Compare with the last 12-month average
• Re-run when new months arrive

steps.say: On a Mac, Python in Excel needs Microsoft 365 on a current version. You insert a Python cell with Control Option Shift P, or from the Formulas tab.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Python in Excel on Mac: Microsoft 365, current channel.
Insert a Python cell: Formulas > Insert Python, or Control + Option + Shift + P.
Code runs in the Microsoft cloud, not on your Mac.

steps.say: To recap. Copilot's advanced analysis writes Python to forecast and cluster. Sanity-check forecasts against recent averages. And read the code: data, scaling, number of groups.

acts.t:
Recap
• “Using Python, …” triggers advanced analysis
• Check forecasts against the last 12-month average
• Read the code: data read, scaling, model settings

steps.say: Your challenge: ask Copilot to check whether Marketing spend and Revenue are correlated, using Python, and confirm it with the CORREL function. Compare with the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
Ask Copilot (Python): how strongly is Marketing spend correlated with Revenue?
Confirm with =CORREL(B2:B37,C2:C37).
Compare with sheet S18-09 Done.
